sources.claim: FCC Declaratory Ruling (February 8, 2024): AI-generated voices in calls count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so such calls need the same prior consent and disclosures as other prerecorded calls.

sections.skill: Recognize AI-assisted scams and verify through a trusted channel

questions.prompt: Why are spelling mistakes a weaker scam sign now?

choices.text: Spelling checks are now illegal
Scammers never use computers
AI can write messages with no mistakes
All real messages contain mistakes

questions.correct_answer: AI can write messages with no mistakes
questions.intro: Scammers use AI too. AI can write convincing messages with no spelling mistakes, imitate a company's style, and CLONE A VOICE from a short recording, so a call can sound like a relative or boss asking for urgent money or gift cards. Old warning signs like bad grammar are less reliable now. Better signs: URGENCY ("act now"), SECRECY ("don't tell anyone"), unusual PAYMENT methods (gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency), and requests for codes or passwords. The strongest defense is to VERIFY THROUGH A TRUSTED CHANNEL: hang up and call the person or company using a number you already know.
questions.feedback: Polished text no longer proves legitimacy.

questions.correct_answer: No; it is the same channel
questions.intro: A CHANNEL is the path a message comes through: a phone number, an email address, a link, a chat. To verify a message, use a DIFFERENT, TRUSTED channel that you already had before the message arrived: the number on the back of your bank card, a contact saved long ago, the company website typed in yourself. Replying to the same email, calling the number in the message, or clicking its link keeps you in the SAME channel, which the sender may control.
questions.feedback: Use a number you already trust.

sections.skill: Prepare defenses against voice and message scams

questions.prompt: A family agrees on a code word for emergencies. How does it help?

choices.text: It lets anyone verify themselves
It stops all robocalls
It makes calls cheaper
A cloned voice will not know the word

questions.correct_answer: A cloned voice will not know the word
questions.intro: Families and workplaces can prepare. Some families agree on a code word for emergencies that a caller must know. Workplaces can require a second person to approve payment changes and a call-back to a known number for any new bank details. Be careful with "verification" that stays inside the scammer's channel: a number or link provided in the suspicious message itself may lead back to the scammer. In the United States, the FCC ruled in 2024 that AI-generated voices in calls count as "artificial" voices under federal robocall rules.
questions.feedback: A shared secret is hard to fake.
